nodes.title: Canvas size
widgets_values:
CANVAS SIZE

canvas_mode decides the resolution H3 generates at:

  manual            - use canvas_width/height exactly as typed
  auto_no_downscale - size from the LARGEST crop in the clip, so no frame is
                      ever downscaled. Can get expensive on clips containing
                      close-ups.
  auto_capped_768   - same, but clamped to 768 (H3's native short edge, and a
                      sane VRAM ceiling). This is what ships here.

canvas_w / canvas_h are WIRED into the H3 node's width/height on purpose. In the auto modes the tracker chooses the size, and if the H3 node disagrees the latent shapes differ and injection refuses. Do not retype them by hand.

Watch the tracker's report for "magnification < 1.0x": that means the crop is being DOWNSCALED into the canvas and real detail is being thrown away. Raise the canvas, or skip the clip if it is close-up throughout.

Cost scales with canvas AREA x frames, so 768 is 2.25x the latent tokens of 512.

nodes.title: Inject Video Latent
widgets_values:
WHY THIS NODE EXISTS

H3's stock nodes ALWAYS build a zeros latent. References are conditioning that is re-injected every step - never a starting point. So there is no video-to-video path out of the box.

This encodes the real cropped frames into the VIDEO stream of the joint AV latent, leaving the audio stream alone. That turns SamplerCustomAdvanced + denoise<1.0 into ordinary img2img.

Frame count must sit on H3's 17k+5 grid (5, 22, 39 ... 175, 226, 362). Clips generated by H3 already do.

nodes.title: Why per-frame crop
widgets_values:
PER-FRAME CROPPING IS MANDATORY

A single fixed crop is sized by the widest frame. On a push-in the face is then STILL SMALL inside that crop - on exactly the frames that needed help. The benefit vanishes where it matters.

So the crop SIZE varies per frame, holding the face at a constant fraction of every crop (crop_factor). Every crop is then resized to ONE canvas, because H3 generates a single fixed WxH for a whole sequence.

Result: the face is always large in H3's input, however small it was in the source.

SMOOTHING
size_smooth_window (51) is deliberately larger than smooth_window (21). Size jitter makes the crop breathe, which changes the resample factor every frame and reads as shimmer.

gaussian beats savgol here - polynomial fits preserve sharp features by design, which is the opposite of what you want.

nodes.title: How lipsync works
widgets_values:
LIPSYNC

H3 is a JOINT audio-video model. NativeAudioLock:
  1. encodes real audio into the AUDIO stream of the AV latent
     (auto-resamples to the VAE's 32kHz - source is usually 48k)
  2. sets noise_mask = ones(video) / zeros(audio)
     so ONLY video denoises
  3. the video branch cross-attends to that fixed audio

That is what shapes the mouth.

Feed it the VOCALS track, not the full mix - cleaner signal.

The ORIGINAL audio goes separately into the save node at the far right. Two different audio paths, do not confuse them.

nodes.title: Stitch + SAM mask
widgets_values:
STITCH + the optional SAM mask

The two nodes to the left - SAMLoader and H3 Face Mask (SAM) - ship MUTED, and stay
wired. Unmute both (Ctrl+M) to swap the rect paste mask for a true face-shaped one.
Muted, this graph needs no SAM model. Unmuted it also needs one, in models/sams/.
ComfyUI-Impact-Pack is required either way: its subpack registers the ultralytics
model folders, and this graph's detector values use that naming.

FEATHER IS IN SOURCE PIXELS, and the two masks want very different values. This graph
ships 24 for the rect. With a SAM mask drop it to 4-8.

KEY POINT: the wide crop exists to give the SAMPLER CONTEXT. It is NOT what gets
pasted. Only the face region composites; everything else keeps its original pixels.

SAM MASKS THE INPUT, NEVER THE OUTPUT. The mask node takes the TRACKER's crops, not
the decoded result - the same way FaceDetailer computes its mask from the source
image. Mask the generated result instead and, if the model nudges the face inward,
the mask traces the NEW smaller silhouette while the original face pokes out past it
- most visibly the nose on profile shots. It is also cheaper: no dependency on the
sampler, so SAM need not be resident alongside the video model.

WORTH KNOWING: a rect mask often BEATS SAM. SAM traces the face tightly, so any drift
in the refined face lands right on the silhouette. A slightly looser rect puts the
seam in hair and background where it reads far less. That is why it is the default.

nodes.title: READ ME FIRST
widgets_values:
WHY THIS EXISTS

MiniMax H3 renders faces poorly when the head is a SMALL FRACTION OF THE FRAME. That is a property of head-size-in-frame, not of resolution - it persists at 720p and above.

So no upscaler fixes it. SeedVR2 and friends sharpen what is already there; they cannot synthesise facial structure that was never generated.

The fix: crop to the face so it fills the frame, let H3 re-generate it at LOW denoise so it stays frame-aligned, then composite back.

nodes.title: Model / encoder
widgets_values:
MODEL AND TEXT ENCODER

Wired: UNETLoader + CLIPLoader, loading pruned int8 weights and an
nvfp4 text encoder. This is the combination these examples were
built and tested against.

Muted beside them: UnetLoaderGGUF + CLIPLoaderGGUF, the GGUF route.
It needs the ComfyUI-GGUF pack, which is why it is not the default
here - but it is a real alternative and fits in less VRAM.

To use GGUF instead: mute the two loaders above, un-mute these two,
and connect UnetLoaderGGUF -> LoraLoaderModelOnly and
CLIPLoaderGGUF -> MiniMax H3 Reference To Video.

Whatever you load, the turbo LoRA and the step count must agree:
the 8-step LoRA wired here wants steps=8 on BasicScheduler. A
4-step LoRA wants 4. Mismatch them and the result is mush or a
waste of time.

nodes.title: Audio source
widgets_values:
AUDIO - drives lipsync

Wired: the audio track of the source clip, straight off the video
loader. That is the simple case and needs nothing extra.

Muted beside it: Load Audio (Upload). Un-mute it and wire its
audio output to BOTH MiniMax H3 Reference To Video and MiniMax H3
Native Audio Lock, in place of the video's own.

Worth doing when you have an isolated VOCAL stem. H3 shapes the
mouth from whatever audio it is given, so a full mix - music,
effects, other voices - is competing with the speech. A vocals-only
track gives cleaner lipsync.

The audio wired here must cover the same stretch of time as the
frames being refined, or the mouth will follow the wrong sound.

nodes.title: DENOISE - read before changing
widgets_values:
DENOISE - THE CRITICAL DIAL

DO NOT carry values over from SDXL-family models. H3 is FLOW MATCHING with a large sigma shift, so the same number means something very different.

sigma = shift*t / (1 + (shift-1)*t)

At the default shift of 12:
  denoise 0.02 -> effective 0.197
  denoise 0.05 -> effective 0.387
  denoise 0.15 -> effective ~0.68
  denoise 0.25 -> effective 0.800

This graph ships denoise 0.40 as a BASE, because it is not applied flat. The H3 Per-Frame Denoise node scales it DOWN per frame by face size: small faces keep close to the full 0.40 and get synthesised, large faces drop to ~0.35x of it and keep the detail they already have.

Base and scaling are tuned TOGETHER. If you bypass the per-frame node, drop the base a long way (0.15-0.25) or every large face gets rewritten.

Too low: nothing changes.
Too high: the head starts drifting relative to the body - a content problem no mask can hide.

NOTE steps and denoise are INDEPENDENT. BasicScheduler builds a (steps/denoise)-long full-range schedule and keeps the lowest steps+1 sigmas, so 8 steps with the turbo LoRA this graph ships is both fast and gentle.

Do NOT use SplitSigmas for this - on a short schedule at shift 12 even the last split point is already sigma 0.800.

nodes.title: Read each clip's own settings
widgets_values:
PER-CLIP SETTINGS

Clips from one batch are often NOT uniform. Read each clip's OWN embedded workflow rather than assuming:

  ffprobe -v error -show_entries format_tags=prompt -of json yourclip.mp4

Things that commonly vary within a single batch: step count, sampler, whether a turbo LoRA was used at all, and how many reference images were attached.

Mirror the clip's own steps / sampler / LoRA / refs here, and change only the denoise settings.

nodes.title: 3. Conditioning + EMPTY AV latent
widgets_values: A young South Asian woman with long dark wavy hair falling past her shoulders, warm medium skin tone, and a small stud earring. She wears a white ribbed tank top with a small multicolor (pink-dominant) floral print, a medium-blue denim mini skirt with two back pockets, and white low-top sneakers. Her build is slim and proportionate; arms rest relaxed at her sides. <Picture 1> locks her full-body front-facing proportion, wardrobe drape, footwear, and serves as the baseline for her side silhouette, natural posture, and back-view body proportions. <Picture 2> anchors her face identity, skin tone, earring, and the floral top's print detail in a three-quarter view, while guiding her profile and back-angle head turns. Both Pictures condition the clip's identity and wardrobe simultaneously across all 360 degrees; no Picture is tied to a specific orbit segment.SUMMARYA single unbroken 12-second 35 mm full-body wide shot of the woman standing on fine pale tropical sand at golden hour. The camera executes a smooth clockwise 360° dolly-orbit at chest height and constant 3–4 m radius, passing from front-on through her left profile, directly behind her, her right profile, and back to front-on. She laughs softly, shifts her weight between feet, and tilts her head to maintain a joyful, open expression throughout. Turquoise surf laps gently behind her; distant palm silhouettes frame the horizon. No cuts, no zoom, no tilt.RETENTION ANALYSISIdentity continuity: Face shape, warm medium skin tone, small stud earring, and long dark wavy hair must remain consistent across all orbit angles, extrapolating her side and back views cleanly from <Picture 2> (primary face) and <Picture 1> (hair length/texture).Wardrobe lock: White ribbed floral tank top, medium-blue denim mini skirt (with two back pockets), and white low-top sneakers must not change, tear, or shift drape unrealistically, holding the front layout of <Picture 1> and logically extending it to the back pockets during the reverse angle.Environment lock: Fine pale sand lower third, turquoise water mid-ground, palm silhouettes and open sky upper background must persist at every orbit angle with no foreground occlusion.Camera lock: Chest-height, 35 mm equivalent, level horizon, subject centered, constant radius—no drift, no zoom, no tilt.Lighting: Warm golden-hour key raking from screen-left in the first half and screen-right in the second half of the orbit; no harsh midday contrast.DETAILED DESCRIPTION0–3 seconds: The camera begins square-on, front-facing, at chest height, 35 mm equivalent, subject centered. Fine pale sand fills the lower third; turquoise surf rolls gently in the mid-background; distant palm silhouettes trace the horizon under a bright, warm sky. The woman stands planted, feet shoulder-width on the sand, arms relaxed at her sides (<Picture 1> front proportion and wardrobe; <Picture 2> face and identity). She gives a soft, genuine laugh, shoulders lifting slightly, head tilting a few degrees to her left. Warm golden-hour light rakes from screen-left, catching the right side of her face and the ribbed texture of her white floral top. The camera begins its smooth clockwise arc, drifting toward her left profile.3–6 seconds: The orbit sweeps through her left side profile and continues toward the position directly behind her. Her long dark wavy hair catches the breeze and lifts slightly off her left shoulder, maintaining the flow and length established in <Picture 1>. She shifts her weight from her right foot to her left, a small grounded rock, and turns her head a few degrees further to the left so her face and joyful smile (<Picture 2>) remain partially visible even as her back grows larger in frame. The turquoise surf and palm silhouettes shift in the background as the camera angle changes. The light, now more frontal from the camera's new vantage, softens across her back and the white of her top.6–9 seconds: The camera passes directly behind her, showing her full back—long dark wavy hair centered down her spine, the two pockets of the denim mini skirt, the ribbed floral top's back drape, and white sneakers planted in the sand, maintaining proportions derived from <Picture 1>. She pivots her head gently to her right, a subtle turn, keeping a bright smile and a glint of her earring (<Picture 2>) visible at the edge of her profile. The camera continues its clockwise sweep toward her right side. Golden-hour light now rakes from screen-right, warming the right contour of her hair and the sand behind her. Surf sound and a light ocean breeze on her hair are the dominant textures.9–12 seconds: The orbit completes its final quadrant, sweeping from her right profile back to square-on front-facing. Her face turns progressively back toward the camera; the full front view re-establishes with <Picture 1> proportion and <Picture 2> identity. She settles her weight back to a neutral stance, both feet planted, arms still relaxed, and offers one last small, warm laugh with her head level. The camera arrives at its starting framing: front-on, full-body, centered, chest-height, 35 mm, level horizon. The end framing is a near-exact match of the opening. Sand, surf, palms, and sky remain unchanged. No cut. The orbit is one continuous, unbroken movement.OVERALL SOUNDSCAPEContinuous natural beach ambience throughout the 12 seconds. Gentle turquoise surf rolling and lapping on pale sand forms the rhythmic bed, slightly closer and more textured when the camera angle brings the water nearer in the background (3–9 seconds). A soft tropical ocean breeze moves through the distant palm fronds, producing a faint, intermittent whisper. The woman's soft, natural laugh is heard twice—once around the 1–2 second mark and again near the 10–11 second mark—warm, close, and unstrained. The subtle shift of her denim skirt and the faint tap of her white sneakers shifting weight on dry sand add small, dry textural accents. No wind gusts, no seagulls, no distant traffic. The soundscape is intimate, warm, and unhurried, matching the slow orbit tempo.NON-DIEGETIC MUSICNo non-diegetic music. The shot carries on natural beach sound and the subject's voice alone; any score or ambient bed is to be layered in post if desired. The H3 prompt should produce only diegetic audio. <Audio 1> is the sound made by the character
